Written gwybod.

word: car → dy gar di; cath → y gath
roman: car -> dy gar di; cath -> y gath
en: soft mutation: the first letter changes after certain words
note: p t c b d g m ll rh soften. After dy, i, o, am, ar, yn (predicative), dau/dwy, and on feminine nouns after y.

word: arna i / arnat ti / arno fe
roman: arna i / arnat ti / arno fe
en: prepositions conjugate for person: ar > arna i, arnat ti, arno fe, arni hi, arnon ni, arnoch chi, arnyn nhw; likewise i fi/iddo fe, wrtha i, amdano fe
note: The single biggest early hurdle - you can't say 'to me' or 'with him' without the right conjugated form.
The everyday spoken form. Fuller: 'mae'n ddrwg 'da fi' (south) / 'gen i' (north).
Often just 'mae'n bwrw'. Heavier: 'mae'n arllwys' or 'pistyllio'. Wales's most-used sentence.
'Da iawn chi' to more than one or to an elder. 'Campus!' and 'Bendigedig!' are stronger praise.
Two words where English has one: mae hi gartre (staying), dw i'n mynd adre (moving). Written gartref/adref. Both appear in other notes but neither is taught.
The sentence that buys patience. Feminine dysgwraig. Soft mutation after yn: dysgwr becomes ddysgwr.

chi: peidiwch â newid i'r Saesneg. Softer: dal ati yn Gymraeg 'da fi, plîs. Welsh speakers switch the second they hear a learner - this is the day-one survival phrase and no Hindi-derived list would ever produce it.

word: Wyt ti'n ...? / Ych chi'n ...? / Yw e'n ...?
roman: Wyt ti'n ...? / Ych chi'n ...? / Yw e'n ...?
note: South: Yw e'n dod? or Odi hi'n dod? (Ydy is North/standard). With ti, speech usually just uses intonation: Ti'n dod? Answer by echoing the verb: Ydw, Odi, Nag ydw. The syllabus teaches the answers (hs-0094) but never the question.

en: not too much for me, thanks

note: Children's word; adults say Mam. Dadi = daddy.

en: bach after a name or kin term = affection, not size
note: Feminine names soft-mutate it: Siân fach, but Tom bach. Same job as cariad, bwt.

en: perfect: Dw i wedi bwyta = I've eaten
note: Swap yn (doing now) for wedi (done). newydd = have just; heb = haven't.

word: o'n i / o't ti / o'dd e
roman: o'n i / o't ti / o'dd e

note: South spoken: o'n i, o't ti, o'dd e/hi, o'n ni, o'ch chi, o'n nhw.

Everyday: shwd un yw e? = what's it like?

Soft mutation after ga i: gofyn becomes ofyn.

Very southern.
Standard hoffi. 'I love it' = dw i wrth fy modd.

en: emphasis: put the key word first, then sy
note: Fi sy'n mynd = I'm the one going. Nos Sadwrn mae'r parti = it's Saturday the party's on.
South hunan, North hun: dy hunan, eich hunan.
ti: wela i di. Wela i chi wedyn = see you later.
ti: edrycha ar dy ôl. Also cadwch yn iawn.
South shortcut: nes i + verb-noun works for any verb (nes i weld). Common short forms: es i, ces i, ath e, wedodd hi.

word: i fi / iddo fe / arna i
roman: i fi / iddo fe / arna i
en: prepositions change shape for each person
note: i fi, i ti, iddo fe, iddi hi, i ni, i chi, iddyn nhw. Same for ar, am, wrth, gyda.
dylwn i, dylet ti, dylai fe + soft mutation.

en: could I have some water, please?
note: Soft mutation after ga i: dŵr becomes ddŵr.

note: South: bant â ni! = off we go.

A pronoun object of a verb-noun takes the possessive: 'ch clywed chi, dy glywed di. 'Clywed chi' is heard but is the anglicised order.
ti: gweld ishe ti. Written: gweld eich eisiau chi.

en: plurals are unpredictable: -au (afal/afalau), -iau, -ion (dyn/dynion), -i (ffenest/ffenestri), vowel change (bachgen/bechgyn); gender shows up as mutation (y ferch but y bachgen, merch fach but bachgen bach)

South pronounces it 'miwn'; ti form dere mewn.

en: what do you do (for a living)?

note: South spoken shortens to 'Ble chi'n byw?'; ti form Ble ti'n byw?
South twym/heddi; North poeth/heddiw. Weather is the default Welsh small talk.

word: Ga i gilo o datws, plîs?
roman: Ga i gilo o datws, plîs?
note: Ga i soft-mutates what follows: cilo > gilo, and o mutates too: tatws > datws.

en: 'will you ...?' - the everyday way to ask someone to do something: Wnei di gau'r drws? Wnewch chi ddod draw?

South spoken (gwddwg); written gwddf.

hwnna (masc) / honna (fem).

The Welsh conversational opener. South shwd/shwt, North sut.

word: Dw i'n cofio / Sa i'n cofio
roman: Dw i'n cofio / Sa i'n cofio
note: sa i = South negative.

Written nesaf. Yr wythnos nesa.
Written diwethaf.

The southern everyday word; north says 'dynes'. Plural 'menywod'.

note: South possession with 'gyda', clipped to ''da'. North: 'sy gynnoch chi'. Soft mutation after 'o': plant becomes blant.

en: have a bite before you go
note: South 'tamed' for 'tamaid'. Nobody leaves a Welsh kitchen unfed.

en: ring me when you get there
note: 'rho ganiad i fi' – give me a ring, very Welsh.
South's word; north 'del'. 'bach' does cute: 'babi bach pert'.

en: two ways to ask 'is there' / 'is it'
note: Oes with something indefinite (Oes bara 'da chi? – Oes), Yw/Ydy with something definite (Yw'r siop ar agor? – Ydy). The commonest learner slip in Welsh, and it decides which yes you get back.

en: nasal mutation: p t c b d g → mh nh ngh m n ng
note: Only after fy and yn: fy nhŷ, fy nghar, fy mrawd, fy nyled; yng Nghaerdydd, ym Mangor, yn Nolgellau. Soft mutation gets its own card (hs-0244) but the other two live only in scattered notes.
The negative past is nowhere in the list. South: nes i ddim + verb-noun works for any verb; also es i ddim, weles i ddim byd. 'Haven't': dw i heb fynd.

Heard constantly, in Welsh and in English. Chwarae teg iddi – fair play to her. South says whare deg.

Signs and addresses are bilingual and the Welsh name is often unrecognisable: Abertawe (Swansea), Casnewydd (Newport), Caerfyrddin (Carmarthen), Aberhonddu (Brecon), Y Fenni (Abergavenny). Soft mutation after i/o: i Gaerdydd, o Gasnewydd.
Spoken fillers: ti'n gwbod, chi'n gweld. 'What does it mean?' = beth yw ystyr ...?
echdoe = the day before yesterday.
All in-laws take -yng-nghyfraith.
Mae e'n perthyn i fi = he's a relative of mine.
Volume/heating. Tro fe lan = turn it up (South lan = up).
The usual question is Faint o'r gloch yw hi?
cofio = to remember; cofia fi at dy fam = give my regards to your mother.

Singular tomato.
South Wales word; North says nionod. Singular winwnsyn.
'da chi = gyda chi (South possession).
South; North mae gen i fol tost.
Fares: pris tocyn / faint yw'r tocyn?
biau = owns; no single word for 'whose'.
In scores you say dim: dau ddim.
Irregular plurals (brawd>brodyr, chwaer>chwiorydd) and aspirate mutation after a: a chwiorydd.
Descriptive only - Welsh has no separate elder-sibling word.
chi is already plural; i gyd adds 'the lot of you'.
Welsh has no all-purpose yes: you echo the verb (Ydw, Oes, Do, Ydy). ie is only for identification questions.
cael bath = have a bath; ymolchi = wash yourself.
South mas; North allan.

en: 'you'd better ...' - the family nudge: Well i ti fwyta nawr, well i ti fynd
note: i ti soft-mutates the verb (bwyta > fwyta). Well i fi fynd = I'd better go.
Cau dy geg! = shut up.
South says yn gwmws for 'exactly'; standard yn union.

en: does this bus go to Swansea?
note: South odi for ydy, as at hs-1038. i takes soft mutation: i Gaerdydd, i Bontypridd (no change on Abertawe).

en: how much will it be to Cardiff?
note: Taxi fare; no haggling culture, the meter decides.
Spoken loan; the tidy word is gwefru.
South gwed (= dwed). Answering the phone: Helô, pwy sy 'na?

South Wales; North del. prydferth = beautiful (tidier).
South (= beth bynnag). gyda llaw = by the way.

note: South spoken drops the R: O'n i'n arfer... arfer literally = to be accustomed.

note: The imperfect. South spoken forms shown; written roeddwn i, roeddet ti...

en: having done: ar ôl bwyta, es i mas
note: Also wrth + verb = while doing; cyn + verb = before doing.
South fy hunan / 'yn hunan; North fy hun. Ar 'y mhen 'yn hunan = on my own.

word: Dw i'n mynd i fod yn hwyr
roman: Dw i'n mynd i fod yn hwyr

note: Also rownd y gornel, ar bwys (South = near).

en: kin terms carry no side or seniority marking: Wncwl Dai, Anti Mair - one word each for uncle and aunt
note: Welsh has one word for uncle and one for aunt, and the person's name does the rest: Wncwl Dai, Anti Mair. No side of the family, no seniority. (Note listed chacha/tau/mama/bua/mausi.)
More idiomatic: dw i'n barod am 'y ngwely.
South Wales; North blin. wedi pwdu = sulking.

Hwyl fawr, wela i di.

Pl. tabledi.
unwaith y dydd, tair gwaith y dydd.

roman: dau ddeg un ... naw deg naw
en: modern decimal counting: dau ddeg un, tri deg pump, naw deg naw; traditional vigesimal still around (un ar hugain, deugain, pedwar ugain); 2/3/4 have feminine forms dwy, tair, pedair

Colloquially twll yn y wal = hole in the wall.
archebu = to order/book anything.
Common in Welsh homes, though nobody minds much; chi form tynnwch eich sgidiau.
South; dolur = a sore.

ti-form; chi-form 'Anfonwch e'. South also says 'hala fe'.

Modern decimal counting, what's taught and mostly said now. Traditional 'un ar hugain' survives for ages and dates.

Soft mutation after 'am': am ddeg, am ddau, am bedwar. 'y bore', 'y prynhawn', 'y nos'.

en: everyone at home, the folks at home
note: 'Shwd mae pawb gartre?' is the standard doorstep enquiry.
South's name for them; elsewhere 'cacen gri' or 'teisen radell'. Off the bakestone, still warm.
'ffa' – beans; 'ffa pob ar dost'.
Grefi ar bopeth; the default with cinio dydd Sul. (Note said 'same role as raita'.)
Literally 'red sauce'; brown sauce is 'saws brown'.

'cloch y drws'. Also in telling time: 'o'r gloch'.

en: to light, to put on (a light or fire)
note: 'cynnau'r tân'. For appliances people say 'rhoi ymlaen'.
Clipped from 'Does dim'. South 'twym'; north 'poeth'.

word: Wyt ti wedi diffodd y nwy?
roman: Wyt ti wedi diffodd y nwy?
en: did you turn the gas off?
note: 'diffodd' – to switch off, put out.
'torri gwallt' – to have a haircut.
'ers' – since, for (a stretch of time up to now).
'ers dyddiau' – for days. 'deuddydd' is the tidy two-day word.
South possession ''da fi'; north 'gen i'.
South 'nawr'; north 'rŵan'.
South 'cer'; north 'dos'. chi-form 'Ewch at y doctor'. Note 'at' for going to a person.

word: Wyt ti wedi cymryd dy dabledi?
roman: Wyt ti wedi cymryd dy dabledi?

note: 'cyn bwyd' – before food.
'rhywbeth at annwyd' – something for a cold. 'at' for what a medicine is for.
'yr un 'na' – that one; 'yr un fach' – the little one (feminine takes the soft mutation).
South 'twym'; north 'poeth'. Weather: 'Mae'n dwym heddi'.
Of people and behaviour: 'paid bod yn gas'. 'gwael' and 'drwg' cover bad in other senses.
'trwchus' for thick things like a book or fog.
Said ''da pwy' in the south. Aspirate mutation: pwy becomes phwy after gyda.
'erbyn' – by (a deadline): 'erbyn dydd Llun'.
Doubles as 'what do you think?' – tone and context separate them.

en: the question / relative / near / far grid
note: Ask with ble, pryd, shwd, pwy; link with lle, pan, fel, sy. (Used 'sut' where the whole syllabus teaches shwd.)
'Mae'n edrych fel glaw' – looks like rain.
Literally 'little people'. The all-purpose surprised exclamation.
Spoken clipping of 'edrychwch'; ti-form 'drycha'.
'gormod' – too much; 'gormod o waith'.
Tagged on the end: 'mae e gartre, siŵr o fod'.

word: Siaradwn ni eto cyn bo hir
roman: Siaradwn ni eto cyn bo hir

note: 'Dw i ar fin gadael' – I'm just about to leave.

en: could I have a word with ...?
note: Used to ask for someone on the phone or at the door.
'gyrru' – to drive, and also to send.
'Pa mor ...?' builds any 'how + adjective' question: pa mor hir, pa mor ddrud.
Clipped from 'Does dim newid gyda fi'.
Nearly always just 'y ffôn'.
'wedyn' – afterwards, later on.
The resigned or wrapping-up shrug, from 'dyna ni'. Consoling and closing both.
The standard answer to 'beth ti'n neud?'
'digon' – enough; 'teg' – fair.
South says 'yn grac' for cross: 'mae Mam yn grac'.
Another 'ar' state, like annwyd and cywilydd.
South's word; north and standard 'crio'.
'gad lonydd iddo' – leave it alone; chi-form 'Gadewch e'.
'chwarter i wyth'. Soft mutation after 'i'.
From 'gwneud y tro'. 'digon da' – good enough.
'ffwrn' is the oven part; many say 'hob' for the rings.
'bag am oes' – bag for life, and you pay for one if you forget it.
Mae'r boeler wedi torri is a sentence you will need in January; boeler combi, gwasanaethu'r boeler. (Note called it 'the equivalent of the geyser'.)
'ffonio'r feddygfa' – ring the surgery, at eight on the dot for an appointment.
'estyn y llaeth i fi' – pass me the milk. The table verb.
'unrhyw beth' – anything; 'unrhyw le' – anywhere.
Dw i ar fin gadael, mae hi ar fin dechrau. South also uses 'jyst â' for almost: 'dw i jyst â starfo'.
The spoken southern default: 'wyt ti'n iwso hwn?'. 'defnyddio' is the standard word.

en: aspirate mutation: p t c → ph th ch
note: Only three letters, and only after a (and), â/gyda, tri, chwe, ei (her), na, tua: mynd â char, ei chartre hi, gwell na choffi, tua thri.

word: dy garu di / ei weld e
roman: dy garu di / ei weld e
en: a pronoun object of a verb-noun becomes a possessive
note: Not caru ti but dw i'n dy garu di; not gweld e but alla i ddim ei weld e; not clywed chi but eich clywed chi. Loose speech does say clywed fi, but you'll hear the tidy form from family all day.
South 'sen i (= taswn i); bydden i'n lico just as common. Softer than dw i moyn, which is what you want when accepting something from a mother-in-law.
Age is missing entirely. Dw i'n bedwar deg oed; mae hi'n dair oed; naw mis oed. chi: faint yw'ch oed chi?
Pob hwyl – all the best, at the end of a message or a call.
chi: cofiwch fi at eich mam. The doorstep sign-off in Welsh-speaking Wales; cofion at the end of a note. Buried in hs-0428's note.
hs-0436 and hs-1114 both say shops here work in pounds, then teach only cilo. Hanner pwys o gig, dau bwys o datws. Pwyso = to weigh.
Welsh has no affectionate address term for her – use her name.
Storm talk more than daily life in Wales.

en: mate, pal (to a man you know)
note: South vocative, from bachgen; also butty/bytty. To a stranger you'd just say esgusodwch fi - Welsh has no bhai-sahab equivalent.
picl a chaws = cheese and pickle.
The table condiment, in place of chutney; sos brown = brown sauce.
pupur = pepper (the vegetable and the seasoning).
A serving dish; dysglaid = a dishful. (Note said 'no equivalent of the thali'.)
A mouthful nobody says; in speech it's teulu Siân or ochr y wraig. (Note referenced sasural.)
Also: nes i dy golli di = I lost you.
y dorf yn y Stadiwm.
Most people just say BP at the surgery.

en: pop it in a bag, please
note: Shop counter. 'plîs' is the everyday spoken borrowing; 'os gwelwch yn dda' is the fuller form.
South says 'beth yw'; north 'be' ydy'.
The south Wales everyday mild exclamation. 'Arglwydd mawr' is stronger.
South 'hunan', north 'hun'. Swap the possessive: ar ben dy hunan, ar ei ben ei hunan.
South says 'heddi' for 'heddiw'.
Mouthful; in speech people say 'mam a thad y wraig'.
'teulu'r gŵr' for the husband's side. This is how it's actually said.
Covers both the sister's husband and the spouse's brother – Welsh doesn't mark whose sibling.
The Hindi item doubles as a swearword; nothing like that here, so the slot takes the missing in-law term.
mam / tad / brawd / chwaer / mab / merch + -yng-nghyfraith. Nasal mutation baked in: cyfraith becomes nghyfraith after 'yn'. No side-of-family marking at all.
Welsh has no standalone 'sir'; formal address is Mr/Mrs + surname, and everything else is first names.
Often written 'Mrs' but said 'Musus' in the valleys. Neutral 'Ms'.
Literally 'flower cabbage'.
Saws persli with ham is the traditional pairing. (Note said 'the coriander slot'.)
Literally 'wine grains'.
'sbeisys' for spices.
'powdwr tsili'.
For undercooked food people usually just say 'heb goginio'n iawn'.
'llysieuol' – vegetarian; 'llysieuwr/llysieuwraig' the person.
No filtering ritual here – tap water is what's drunk and offered.
Gwybed mân = midges, a real problem on a summer evening; cleren = a fly (South). (Note said 'mosquitoes aren't a thing here'.)
'ysgub' is the formal word for a broom.
'anadlu' – to breathe; 'mas o wynt' – out of breath.
'Mae'r bendro arna i' – I'm dizzy. Another of the 'ar' ailments.
Everyday speech prefers 'wedi brifo' or south 'dolur'.
'taflu lan' is the colloquial 'throw up'.
More natural than the literal 'gorffwyswch'.
'tacsi' is the general word; outside the cities it's a phone call to the local firm.
Usually said as 'mae'r traffig yn ofnadwy'.
South 'odi' for 'ydy'.
Most people say 'contactless' or 'talu ar y ffôn'.
'hanner pris' – half price; 'bargen' – a bargain.

word: Alla i ddim dy weld di
roman: Alla i ddim dy weld di
note: 'mae'r llun wedi rhewi' – the picture's frozen.
South Wales staple, mild but not for chapel. 'Yffach gols!' is the full version.
Everyday, not blasphemous. South also 'sa i'n gwbod, wir' – I really don't know.
'wrth y goleuadau' – at the lights.
The resigned shrug in question form.
For nil or nothing you say 'dim': 'dim i ddim' – nil-nil.
'cant a hanner' also heard. 'can' before a noun: 'can punt'.
'yr henoed' is the collective term used by services and the chapel.
Butchers and markets here still work in pounds: 'hanner pwys o gig'.
'chwysu' – to sweat.
Shoes off at the door is normal here too.
'pen-blwydd' alone is a birthday.

Chapel life: mynd i'r angladd, y gwasanaeth. Cydymdeimladau – condolences; meddwl amdanoch chi. Priodas is taught and this isn't, though with older Welsh-speaking neighbours it comes round more often.
